title: Starting the workday
hook: a breath and an intention before work

segments.voice: Yesterday, the craftsman's devotion: shokunin, and Ben Sira's smith at his anvil. Your line was a bit better. Which corner met a little cleaner? Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A Roman emperor, writing notes to himself, admits he doesn't want to get out of bed. That's how the fifth book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations begins: in the morning, when you rise unwillingly. Today the scene looks different and sounds familiar. The laptop opens, the inbox loads, and the first stretch of the day is gone before a single choice has been made. Several traditions put something small at that doorway. Today: Marcus Aurelius.
screen: `AN EMPEROR WHO WON'T GET UP.` → `THE INBOX LOADS.` → `SOMETHING AT THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: First, Marcus. His answer to himself is blunt: remember that you are rising to do the work of a human being. Why grumble about doing the very thing you exist for? Were you made to lie under the blankets and keep warm? Then he points outside: the little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, each working at its part of the world. Second, a psalm. Psalm 90 carries the heading a prayer of Moses, and its last verse, in the King James Bible, is a request about work: "and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it." The request comes twice in one verse, as if once weren't enough. If you pray, it's a line already made for the start of a workday. Third, a doorway from Islam. A hadith in the collection of Abu Dawud tells of words the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught for leaving the house: in the name of God, I put my trust in God, there is no might and no power except with God. Bismillah, in the name of God, is a phrase Muslim practice sets at the start of ordinary things, a meal, a journey, a task. Fourth, the breath. The Vietnamese teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught people to stop and breathe before ordinary acts, even before picking up a ringing phone. Put these together and you get a very small practice. Not a ritual to adopt, just a doorway between the rest of life and the job: one breath, then one sentence. What is this work for, today? Then open the inbox.
screen: `RISING TO A HUMAN'S WORK.` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.` · `IN THE NAME OF GOD.` · `ONE BREATH, ONE SENTENCE.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH A BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and picture the place where your work begins: a desk, a counter, a car, a kitchen, a classroom. Before anything opens, take one full breath, slower than usual, and let it out all the way. Then name, silently, the work ahead in a few words. Then one intention for it: careful, kind, patient, brave, whatever fits. If you pray, you can use a line your tradition already has, like the psalm's or the bismillah. Then let the picture go, and simply breathe. The bell holds the time.
Marcus Aurelius. The Roman emperor who told himself, rising unwillingly, that he was made for the work of a human being. Today's word.
Your line: begin with a breath. Before you open the first message or pick up the first tool, take one full breath and name what the work is for. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims begin ordinary acts with bismillah, in the name of God; some Jews and Christians pray Psalm 90:17 over their work; readers of Marcus Aurelius return to Meditations 5.1 on hard mornings.

notes: Meditations 5.1 paraphrased (Long 1862 wording not quoted): rising unwillingly, the work of a human being, the blankets, the plants, birds, ants, spiders and bees. 'A notebook meant only for himself' describes the Meditations as private writing; confirm or soften.

Abu Dawud 5095 (the supplication on leaving the house: bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah) paraphrased; an Islam Keeper should confirm the number and wording. 'Muslims begin a great many ordinary things with bismillah' is a general practice claim; confirm or soften.
Thich Nhat Hanh is named and paraphrased (pausing to breathe before answering the telephone), never quoted; confirm the attribution.
Psalm 90 heading: 'A Prayer of Moses the man of God' (KJV superscription).

Editor: 'a notebook meant only for himself' softened to 'writing notes to himself' (the text doesn't say it was private); 'a phrase Muslims use to begin ordinary things' recast as what Muslim practice sets before a meal, a journey, a task; review line updated to Ben Sira's smith to match the edited day 921.
Audit: Psalm 90:17 (KJV), Meditations 5.1 and Abu Dawud 5095 checked; no changes.
